The ration record describes the distribution, the stele records the victory, and the household absorbed the difference between what was demanded and what remained.

There was no single invention of organised war. In southern Mesopotamia, temple accounts made labour and food available to institutions that could outlast individual supervisors. At Lagash, the disputed boundary with Umma became a sacred and royal cause represented on the Stele of the Vultures. In Egypt, the Narmer Palette turned the defeated enemy and the king’s blow into parts of an ordered image of rule. Around Uruk and across Akkadian territories, rations and deportations carried political demands into ordinary lives. Storage, writing, ranked offices, sacred claims, and territorial competition reinforced one another without producing the same form of violence everywhere.

The record shows organised coercion through its objects: clay marked with quantities, stone carved with ranks, palettes divided into registers, and inscriptions that made conquest a claim about rightful order. It does not show that urban people were more aggressive by nature than communities who lived before cities. What changed was the ability of particular rulers and offices to direct labour, preserve decisions, and connect resources to force. A wall could keep an enemy out while its construction consumed household labour. A storehouse could feed workers while binding them to an institution. A king could turn a border into a sacred duty and a captive population into a labour supply. Around Uruk, Lagash, and the territories ruled by Akkadian kings, the city made those powers durable, and durability carried violence beyond the day on which it was used.

chapters.title: Empires and the Management of Difference
chapters.markdown:
The Assyrian king’s inscription does not begin with a tax table or a provincial office. It begins with conquest. Cities are captured and populations are carried away; the language joins military victory to the authority of the god Ashur. An Assyrian deportation inscription may enumerate towns destroyed, peoples removed, livestock seized, and tribute imposed, presenting the king’s violence as proof that resistance would bring punishment while submission preserved a place within the imperial order. That evidence has encouraged a durable interpretation of Assyria as a state whose rule rested only on fear. The interpretation has force. Assyrian armies destroyed rebellious settlements, mutilated enemies, and displayed defeated rulers in ways intended to instruct spectators. The inscriptions were royal declarations, placed in palaces and public settings, and their vocabulary repeatedly joined military victory to the king’s legitimacy. A ruler who wanted subjects to understand the cost of revolt had reason to describe revolt in memorable and frightening terms. Yet an empire governed only through terror would have had to terrorize every village, every harvest, every caravan, and every local official without interruption. The surviving deportation lists suggest something more exacting and more ordinary. They record people assigned to places, occupations, and communities within an imperial system. A population removed from one region was not simply erased. It was counted, transported, settled, and made available for work or military service elsewhere. The brutality of deportation lay partly in this administrative afterlife: a conquered person remained useful to the state that had displaced him.

The list changes the meaning of the conquest inscription. A royal account can say that a city was humbled; an administrative record can show households divided, specialists relocated, and people attached to new settlements. The first speaks in the language of victory. The second follows the consequences into offices and fields. Both belong to the same rule. Assyria needed fear to discourage rebellion, but it also needed roads, stores, scribes, governors, and communities that could continue producing after the army had gone. This does not make Assyrian rule mild. Deportation was violent even when the destination was fertile and the assigned work secure. Families lost houses, fields, graves, local shrines, and the knowledge of whom to trust. A person moved from the Levant to the lands of the Tigris did not arrive as a free migrant choosing a better livelihood. The movement followed defeat and the decision of the king. Where the inscription’s numbers survive, they convert suffering into an achievement of command. Nor does administration replace terror. Public punishment could make a governor’s demand credible; the governor could then collect grain without sending soldiers to every field. A deportation could break a local coalition while supplying labour to another province. A protected temple could preserve a city’s ritual life while its treasury supported the crown. Rule was not divided between violence and accommodation. It joined them according to place, status, and political need.

Ashurnasirpal II could boast of terror at Kalhu and still depend on scribes who recorded deliveries, officials who supervised settlements, and local elites who translated imperial commands into familiar obligations. The palace relief and the deportation list show different surfaces of the same state. One magnifies the king’s power. The other distributes it through names, quantities, routes, and assignments. Read alone, the first makes Assyria appear to be a machine of exemplary cruelty, while the second allows the human violence of conquest to disappear into paperwork. The evidence requires both.

An army could take a city once. Officials had to turn that seizure into annual grain, labour, obedience, and information. Terror opened the way, but records and intermediaries kept the way open.

Imperial rule drew on a repertoire: tribute in silver, livestock, grain, timber, textiles, or military assistance; deportation to weaken rebellious communities and redirect labour; roads for armies, messengers, merchants, and collectors; censuses that made households legible; hostages who attached a ruler’s promise to the bodies of relatives; local governors who supervised districts; and protected cults that allowed conquered communities to retain temples and rites under conditions acknowledging imperial supremacy. Each device joined a political purpose to a material one. A road moved troops, but it also moved reports. A census identified taxpayers, but it also identified the households officials could summon.

The Assyrian deportation lists reveal the precision behind a practice often described only as mass removal. A list could distinguish groups by origin, occupation, or destination. A craft worker was not interchangeable with a farmer; a skilled metalworker might be sent where the palace required specialised production, while agricultural households were settled on land needing cultivation. The record treated movement as an allocation problem. It made human displacement serve the needs of a court that could reach across several hundred miles.

The king’s inscription supplied the threat that made such movement intelligible. A defeated people had not merely changed address. They had been broken by the god-backed ruler and reassigned by his command. The list supplied the quieter continuation, when wagons had to be organised, rations provided, land assigned, and officials informed. Deportation was at once punishment, population policy, and labour management.

Achaemenid rule used a different imperial grammar. The satrap stood between the Great King and the province, collecting revenues, hearing reports, commanding troops, and negotiating with local power holders. The satrapal administration did not require every region to resemble the Persian heartland. Lydia could retain its language, sanctuaries, aristocratic families, and urban traditions while contributing wealth and obedience to the empire. The king’s authority reached the province through offices that were Persian in loyalty but often dependent on local knowledge.

Tribute was not simply the price of peace. It was a recurring declaration that the province belonged to the king. Payments crossed the distance between Sardis and the imperial court, tying local production to a larger political geography. Once tribute was assessed, collected, and delivered, the conquered region became a fiscal unit whose people and resources could be anticipated from year to year.

The route from Sardis toward the interior and beyond gave that expectation a physical form. It allowed couriers to move orders and reports, merchants to travel under imperial protection, and officials to carry information between local offices and the court. A road did not compel obedience by itself. Its value depended on guards, stations, animals, supplies, and rules of passage. The imperial road system joined these practical requirements to the political demand that distant events be made known.

Censuses performed similar work on a smaller scale. To count land or households was to identify who could be charged, summoned, or protected. A register could support tribute, organised labour, or the settlement of a dispute between a village and an official. Counting did not create the obligation, but it gave the obligation a durable reference. A household that had been recorded could be found again.

Hostages narrowed the space for local independence. A provincial ruler might retain office, wealth, and ceremonial dignity while sending a son or another relative to the imperial court. The hostage placed the family’s future inside the king’s reach and exposed the local ruler to the habits and expectations of the imperial centre. A promise made by a governor acquired force because its violation could injure someone close to him.

Local governors and intermediary offices carried imperial demands into settings the court could not directly observe. A village headman knew which families possessed animals; a city magistrate knew which merchants could advance silver; a temple official knew which lands supported the sanctuary; an aristocratic landholder knew which rival might turn a tax demand into revolt. Such figures did not merely transmit orders. They selected translators, measured compliance, concealed or revealed resources, and bargained over the cost of enforcement.

Protected cults allowed difference to survive under supervision. Persian kings could present themselves as patrons of temples in lands whose gods were not Persian gods. Destroying every local shrine would have multiplied enemies and disrupted institutions that already organised land, labour, and trust. A temple could continue its rites while its priesthood recognised the imperial order, paid what was required, and avoided supporting rebellion.

Rome developed these techniques across an even more varied territory. Roads cut through Britain, Gaul, Anatolia, North Africa, and the Near East, but they did not have one meaning in every place. In Britain, a road could carry a legion toward a troubled frontier, connect a fort to a town, or support the movement of officials and goods. Its paving stones and drainage ditches belonged to military logistics, yet towns grew along routes that also carried civilian exchange. A structure built to secure conquest could later support forms of life that were not reducible to war.

The Roman census made provincial populations available to taxation and service. Officials sought to identify land, property, citizenship, and status, categories that determined what a person owed and what protections a person could claim. Roman law offered a language for petitions and contracts, but it operated within a hierarchy distinguishing citizens, non-citizens, slaves, allies, and subjects. A census could make claims more regular while also making extraction more exact.

A Roman governor could not personally inspect every estate, market, or village. Municipal councils, tax contractors, landowners, priests, interpreters, and military suppliers converted commands into transactions. The empire appeared in a town through a magistrate’s decree, a tax demand, a road repair, a court hearing, or the arrival of soldiers. Imperial government was encountered locally, often through people whose families had ruled or prospered before the conquest. The same repertoire could protect and threaten. A road reduced travel time for a merchant and shortened the march of troops. A census clarified a land claim and fixed a taxable obligation. A hostage prevented revolt and turned a child into a guarantee. A governor settled a feud and appropriated the power to decide whose account counted. A protected cult preserved a community’s identity while binding its leaders to the sovereign who offered protection.

A province became governable when these practices worked together. Tribute required a count; a count required local knowledge; local knowledge moved through roads; roads required officials and protection; protection depended on a continuing flow of revenue. The imperial state did not need to erase every difference. It needed to arrange difference so that separate peoples could be made to pay, report, serve, and remain available.

Roman Britain and Achaemenid Lydia present two provinces shaped by this problem, though they did not receive the same solution. Britain lay at the uncertain western edge of Roman power, where conquest remained contested and the frontier demanded forts, roads, and repeated military attention. Lydia occupied an older urban and agricultural region in western Anatolia, where the Persians could rule through the existing prominence of Sardis and the networks of local elites who already connected countryside, city, and sanctuary.

Military construction was conspicuous in Britain. Forts, roads, walls, and clustered settlements marked the presence of soldiers and the material requirements of their supply. The province had to be held against resistance beyond the settled zone, and the army was not a distant symbol. Its camps consumed food, animals, timber, labour, and transport. A road from a fort could serve commerce, but its first importance lay in allowing Rome to reinforce positions and move men through territory recently conquered.

Lydia’s position inside the Achaemenid world produced a different imperial landscape. Sardis had been the capital of the Lydian kingdom and remained an important centre under Persian rule. The province’s value rested on cultivated land, urban wealth, routes through western Anatolia, and access to the Aegean. The Persian king did not need to construct a new political world from the ground upward. He could govern through an established city, local aristocracies, temple communities, and officials whose knowledge of the region predated the conquest.

The difference was visible in the relationship between conquest and infrastructure. Roman Britain required the empire to build an extensive military presence in a region where Roman rule was recent and vulnerable. Achaemenid Lydia allowed the empire to appropriate an existing centre whose roads, revenues, and social hierarchies already had deep local roots. Persia still required tribute and supervision, and Lydia could still become a site of revolt or dynastic conflict. The costs of control were distributed differently.

The two provinces also differed in the form through which belonging was negotiated. In Britain, the Roman army stood as an occupying and organising institution. Auxiliary soldiers recruited from different regions served in units stationed far from their original homes, while local communities encountered Roman power through forts, towns, taxation, and law. Cultural change followed, but unevenly. A household near a military centre did not experience Rome in the same way as a settlement farther from the roads.

Persian rule could leave more room for local continuity in Lydia because the province already possessed a powerful urban and ceremonial history. Sardis did not become meaningless when Croesus was defeated. Its old significance became a resource that successive rulers could use. The Persian king’s government depended on the city’s position rather than requiring its complete replacement. Local officeholders could preserve status by serving a new monarch, and the population could continue many practices while paying into a different imperial treasury. Neither case fits a simple opposition between violent occupation and peaceful accommodation. Britain’s forts provided security for some travellers and danger for others; Roman courts could regulate disputes while taxes and requisitions strained households. Lydia’s local elites retained influence, but that influence was conditional on imperial loyalty and could expose subordinate communities to demands negotiated above them. Accommodation did not remove coercion. It relocated much of it.

A road in Britain and a route near Sardis could both carry soldiers and revenue, yet the surrounding political conditions gave them different effects. In Britain, the road helped make a contested frontier accessible to Roman force. In Lydia, routes joined a wealthy province to an imperial network that could draw on older centres of production and exchange. The physical technology was comparable; the historical task was not. Technology extended reach, but institutions and local choices determined whom that reach served.

The comparison also warns against treating provincial populations as passive recipients of empire. British communities could resist, collaborate, negotiate, abandon settlements, or use Roman categories for local advantage. Lydian elites could preserve authority by brokerage, compete for office, or present themselves as indispensable to the Persian king. The imperial centre required local action even when it described provincial obedience as the result of royal power alone.

Revenue made these relationships concrete. Conquest became durable when grain, silver, labour, and information began to arrive through predictable channels. A province that paid regularly could retain more local forms. A province that delayed or revolted invited military intervention. The balance between accommodation and coercion changed with the reliability of the flow.

Roman tax farming shows how the conversion occurred at close range. The state could assign the right to collect certain taxes to contractors who advanced money or purchased the contract, then recovered their outlay from provincial taxpayers with a profit. The contractor’s interest was immediate. The Roman treasury wanted revenue at the expected time; the contractor wanted more from the province than had been paid for the privilege of collection. Between the two stood local communities, landholders, merchants, and households whose liabilities had to be assessed and enforced.

A tax farmer therefore needed information and cooperation. He needed to know who owned land, which goods crossed a market, what a town could pay, and which local notable could bring reluctant taxpayers before an official. He might employ agents, rely on municipal councils, and negotiate with influential families. Soldiers remained available when negotiation failed, but ordinary collection depended on a dense local chain rather than constant military seizure. That chain could make taxation more efficient and more oppressive. A collector who exceeded the agreed demand could enrich himself, reward allies, or compensate for losses. A local council could distribute the burden towards poorer residents while protecting its own property. A landowner could advance money and recover it from tenants. Roman law might provide a route for complaint, but access to courts required time, money, status, and a person able to present the case in the empire’s language.

The tax farmer’s violence was often indirect. He did not need to strike every debtor. The threat of confiscation, arrest, forced sale, or military intervention could make a demand effective before physical force appeared. Economic pressure became destructive through the political definition of liability and the unequal ability to resist it. A shortage, a bad harvest, or a delayed payment could turn an ordinary obligation into the loss of animals, tools, land, or freedom.

Achaemenid tribute followed a different institutional path. The satrap governed a province whose annual contribution was connected to its assessed wealth and place within the empire. Lydia’s wealth, associated with Sardis and western Anatolia, could be directed towards the king through officials who understood local production and routes. Tribute was not gathered by an abstract empire hovering above the countryside. It passed through provincial households, city authorities, estates, temples, and agents.

The satrap occupied a dangerous position. He had to satisfy the king without allowing the province to become ungovernable, and he possessed enough military and fiscal power to threaten the king’s interests if he turned that power towards independence. The court therefore required reports, rival channels of information, and the presence of royal officers alongside the satrap. The province was governed through delegation, but delegation was watched.

A village or city did not experience the satrap’s annual obligation as a single payment made by one office. The demand was broken into assessments and claims. A city might draw on its treasury, landholders, merchants, or temple resources. Local leaders could negotiate timing, identify exemptions, or shift the cost towards people with less influence. In a province with old aristocratic families, brokerage became a form of power. The family that could secure favourable terms from the satrap gained standing at home; the satrap gained a dependable partner.

Brokerage worked because the imperial centre lacked complete knowledge. A royal order could specify the tribute expected, but it could not reveal every field, debt, feud, or hidden store. Local intermediaries supplied information while shaping it. They translated imperial categories into local relationships and local grievances into language the court might accept. A ruler who appeared obedient might be protecting his town from a greater demand, or he might be using the king’s name to defeat a rival.

The provincial elite did not stand outside extraction. They often received a share of its benefits. Land, contracts, offices, and access to officials could enrich families willing to serve the empire. Their position depended on maintaining two audiences: the imperial ruler, who required revenue and loyalty, and the local population, whose compliance could not be assumed. A successful intermediary made imperial demands seem compatible with local hierarchy. An unsuccessful one exposed the empire’s dependence on force.

The arrangement could be cruel precisely because it was negotiated. A community might be spared the destruction of a siege and still lose part of its harvest each year. A local ruler might retain his title while sending relatives as hostages. A merchant might gain protection on an imperial road while paying fees and taxes that narrowed his margin. A temple might keep its rites while surrendering land, silver, or labour. The absence of mass killing did not mean the absence of coercion.

Recurring revenue did not require every subject to regard the empire as foreign. Roman Britain produced people who adopted Roman names, served in Roman units, traded through Roman towns, and sought advantage within Roman law. Lydia retained local traditions while participating in Persian kingship. Belonging could be layered. A person might identify with a town, a cult, a language community, a royal household, and an imperial order, with the balance changing according to circumstance. These layered affiliations helped states restrain some private violence. Courts, governors, and municipal officials could intervene in disputes that might otherwise become feuds. A road protected by soldiers could reduce the danger of banditry for travellers. A census could clarify inheritance or property claims. A local governor could punish an armed faction before it grew. The same offices that reduced private retaliation made it possible to collect taxes from a wider population and mobilise larger forces against those classified as rebels.

The scale of harm changed when the channels were joined. Tribute supplied the treasury, which paid soldiers who guarded roads and enforced judgments. Roads brought orders and troops. Censuses identified taxpayers and recruits. Local intermediaries converted imperial categories into village demands. Protected cults gave the arrangement a degree of legitimacy. Deportation supplied labour where conquest or construction required it. None of these practices alone explains an empire; their combination made distant rule routine.

A province could therefore be both protected and exposed. The empire promised order against raiders, rivals, and local magnates while reserving the right to define resistance as rebellion. It offered continuity to a temple or council while taking the surplus that sustained that continuity. It restrained one kind of aggression by authorising another. The crucial question was who could invoke the state, who could be heard by it, and whose losses counted as the cost of peace.

The Assyrian inscription, the Persian satrapal system, and the Roman provincial record belong to different political worlds. They should not be collapsed into a single imperial model. Assyria used deportation on a scale and with a rhetoric that served its own military monarchy. Achaemenid kingship relied heavily on satraps, royal roads, provincial tribute, and the preservation of local forms. Rome developed its own combination of citizenship, municipal government, military occupation, legal status, and tax collection. Comparison becomes useful when it follows the specific operation rather than assuming that every empire meant the same thing by rule.

In each case, conquest produced a choice between withdrawal and continued administration. Withdrawal left a border, a city, or a captured population to reorganise itself. Continued administration demanded officials, records, supplies, and explanations for why the conqueror’s demands were lawful. Violence established the relationship, but repeated revenue and managed difference maintained it. The people subject to that relationship did not become less human because a scribe counted them. They became more exposed to decisions made far away.

An inscription could celebrate the king’s enemies as broken. A deportation list could assign them a destination. A road could bring the order, and a governor could bargain over its cost. A census could find the household that owed it, while a temple could sanctify the settlement that followed. Empire endured through this sequence, in which exceptional violence became an ordinary claim on land, labour, movement, and loyalty.

chapters.title: Warriors, Cities, and Moral Order in the Americas
chapters.markdown:
A tribute system becomes visible in the things it had to move. Maize, beans, cotton cloth, cacao, feathers, rubber, copper, stone, and finished goods did not travel toward Tenochtitlan by themselves. Someone assessed a province, gathered its contribution, carried it along a road or across a lake, and received it at a storehouse or court. At its height in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, the Mexica empire depended on this repeated passage from conquered communities to the island capital. Its power was reproduced whenever a provincial town delivered what officials expected and whenever an official could identify the town that had failed.

The tribute rolls associated with Mexica administration record that process with unusual clarity. They organize obligations by place and commodity, linking named provinces to quantities of cloth, food, weapons, garments, and luxury goods. A roll does not describe every village household or reveal what each taxpayer thought of the demand. It shows conquest converted into a schedule. A community that had once faced a war party now faced a recurring obligation, divided among local authorities and calculated in units that could be checked.

The first step was political submission. A city defeated by the Triple Alliance—Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, and Tlacopan—might retain its ruler, temples, markets, and internal officials while acknowledging the alliance and providing tribute. The Mexica did not govern every province through an identical office or a uniform garrison. Local rulers and subordinate nobles remained useful because they knew fields, storehouses, kinship ties, and rivalries. They could collect goods more cheaply than an army stationed among strangers.

From the provincial town, the demand passed through households and local offices. Cotton was spun and woven before it could appear as a bundle of cloth. Maize had to be grown, harvested, dried, stored, and carried. A cloak or shield required labor from people who might never see Tenochtitlan. Tribute was a claim on time as well as on objects, reaching into agricultural seasons, craft production, transport, and the authority of local men who decided how the burden would be distributed.

The goods converged on the capital, where their uses multiplied. Food provisioned officials, workers, and warriors. Cloth could clothe soldiers or be redistributed as reward. Feathers, precious stones, and finely worked objects entered ceremonies in which imperial abundance became visible. A tribute roll turned distant production into an account; the capital turned that account into sustenance, payment, and display. Goods that marked provincial dependence could also bind Mexica followers to the imperial center.

Captive-taking fitted this system because war supplied both people and meaning. Mexica warfare did not serve one purpose in every campaign. Battles could secure tribute, punish disobedience, extend influence, obtain captives, or strengthen the standing of nobles and warriors. Captives were not simply another commodity, though captivity could involve labour, sale, ransom, or incorporation into households. A warrior who seized an enemy alive acquired a public record of achievement, and that success could alter his rank, dress, privileges, and access to honour.

Taking a captive required a different violence from killing an enemy in flight. The captor had to overpower, restrain, and preserve the person who might otherwise have been struck down. Mexican pictorial traditions distinguish warriors by insignia and record prisoners through bound figures and formal gestures. The experience varied with rank, battlefield circumstance, and later use, but the practice joined bodily danger to social recognition. A warrior’s reputation could be built through acts that the state and the temple were prepared to remember.

A captive brought toward Tenochtitlan entered a sequence in which the military event became a civic and religious performance. Processions, public ceremonies, the clothing of priests and rulers, the handling of weapons, and the presentation of captives made conquest visible to people who had not fought in the campaign. The capital’s sacred precinct was not separate from imperial politics. Its buildings, stairways, stone images, drums, and courts gave domination a moral vocabulary in which victory could appear as service to the gods and protection of the ordered world.

The Great Temple, or Templo Mayor, rose at the centre of that world. Its paired sanctuaries associated Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc with Mexica warfare, rain, agriculture, and the city’s sacred identity. The staircase and summit arranged the ceremony vertically: crowds below, priests and rulers above, and captives brought into a space where military success could be interpreted as cosmic duty. Human sacrifice occurred within this ritual order, but it should not be detached from the political setting that made captives available and their display meaningful.

The ceremonies helped produce the reasons for acquiring captives again. A ruler who received tribute could finance military action; military action brought captives and new claims; captives could be used in rituals that demonstrated the ruler’s service to the gods; the demonstration reinforced his authority over nobles, soldiers, and provinces. The sequence was practical and symbolic at once.

Tenochtitlan’s island setting sharpened the need for organization. Causeways connected the city to the mainland, canals carried people and goods, and markets concentrated exchange. A provincial contribution arriving by canoe or over a causeway could be inspected, stored, redistributed, or incorporated into a ceremony. The capital’s scale did not make violence inevitable, but it allowed distant coercion to become urban routine and sustained campaigns beyond the immediate basin.

The tribute rolls reveal administrative reach through their classifications. Provinces appear as contributors with particular obligations, not as undifferentiated enemies. A place could be conquered and then made legible: its name, goods, and expected quantities entered a system in which failure could be recognized and answered. The memory of a prior defeat could carry the threat of renewed force into years when no army was present. That threat was uneven. The Triple Alliance did not possess a modern bureaucracy that penetrated every household, and tribute did not erase local politics. Some territories remained difficult to control. Tlaxcala resisted Mexica expansion and became a major ally of the Spanish in 1519. Other communities negotiated, rebelled, or used imperial rivalries for their own purposes. A tribute schedule shows an expected relationship, while the effort required to maintain it reveals how much administration depended on local cooperation.

A provincial ruler who collected tribute could protect his position by presenting himself as the necessary broker between town and empire. He could also direct burdens toward weaker households or withhold information from the imperial centre. Mexica rule restrained certain forms of private raiding and feud by placing them beneath a larger political order, while authorizing the centre and its local partners to take goods, labour, and people on a wider scale. The capital’s peace was purchased through obligations that were peaceful only in their outward form.

The stone and stucco of the sacred precinct made that relationship public. A captive led through the city came from a place, belonged to a people, and had been seized in a campaign whose consequences reached households far from the temple. The ceremony compressed those histories into an image of Mexica victory. The individual body became evidence of an order that claimed to feed the gods, protect the city, and place conquered communities in their proper relation to Tenochtitlan.

Across the Maya lowlands, political order was more fragmented. Dos Pilas offers a portrait of a polity that had to make danger visible before it could be contained. Its monuments and inscriptions preserve the careers of rulers through dates, titles, victories, accessions, and ritual acts. The stones do not give a neutral account of the kingdom. They show how a royal court wanted later generations to understand its right to rule.

Dos Pilas stood in the Petexbatun region of what is now Guatemala, near the Pasión River, within the wider rivalry among Maya centres. The city was founded in the seventh century by Bajlaj Chan K’awiil, whose inscriptions connect him to the dynasty of Tikal. His authority at Dos Pilas therefore carried a history of kinship and separation. He was not an anonymous warlord outside political tradition. The monuments placed him within a royal lineage while recording the violence through which that lineage established a second centre.

Bajlaj Chan K’awiil’s inscriptions describe conflict with Tikal through the formal language of Maya kingship. Dates placed victories and rituals in calendrical order, connecting political action to dynastic time. A ruler’s legitimacy depended on more than winning a battle. He had to show that accession, ceremony, and victory belonged to a sequence inherited from ancestors and sanctioned by the gods.

The early monuments at Dos Pilas present this claim in stone. Stelae carried the ruler’s image, costume, titles, and dates; hieroglyphic texts named places and described events in which his body stood at the centre of history. An enemy defeated elsewhere could be brought into the city through words and carved signs. The monument made a campaign durable, allowing a political act to outlast the people who had witnessed it.

For a time, Dos Pilas gained strength through alliance with Calakmul, Tikal’s great rival. That alignment belonged to a regional struggle in which Maya polities competed for trade routes, subordinate communities, prestige, and strategic position. The wars were not the expression of one unified Maya state. Each centre had its own court, rulers, dependencies, and calculations. Dos Pilas mattered because its dynasty could convert a vulnerable location into a node within a larger contest.

The city’s walls make the portrait harder to read. Defensive works were built and expanded around Dos Pilas, and archaeological evidence indicates that the settlement was fortified in the later period of its history. The walls include earthworks and ditches that altered approaches to the site. Their presence suggests apprehension about attack, but it does not identify the attacker or tell us whether the works protected the royal precinct, the wider population, or a reduced population gathered under pressure.

A wall required labour before it became protection. Soil had to be cut and carried, embankments raised, passages controlled, and vulnerable approaches considered. In a landscape of seasonal rains and difficult movement, a defensive line could also mark the limits of a community’s capacity to hold ground. Labour that had sustained palaces and monuments could be redirected towards survival. Dos Pilas’s walls show a court responding to danger with organized work, though the stones preserve none of the workers’ voices.

The inscriptions continue to speak in the names of kings. Later rulers recorded accessions and ceremonies even as the region became more unstable. The dynastic record sought continuity, while the defensive earthworks imply a political world in which continuity was uncertain. A court that carved its history and fortified its settlement was making the same claim in different materials: the dynasty remained capable of ordering people, land, memory, and defence.

Then the city was abandoned. The end did not arrive as a single event preserved in a complete narrative. Archaeology shows a settlement whose public life ceased, whose monuments remained, and whose buildings were no longer maintained as an active royal centre. Some monuments were deliberately broken or altered, and the destruction of political images may have accompanied the collapse of the dynasty. The surviving texts continue to name rulers whose authority had already become past.

Dos Pilas does not demonstrate that Maya kings were uniquely warlike, or that warfare alone caused the city’s decline. It shows a polity in which dynastic identity, regional alliance, monument building, and defensive construction answered one another. A ruler needed warriors to win recognition; recognition helped command labour; labour raised monuments and walls; monuments justified the ruler’s claim; walls testified that the claim was under threat. The sequence resembles the joined fiscal and military processes visible at Tenochtitlan, but its scale, political geography, and evidence remain distinct.

A carved date can make a king’s action precise. It cannot make his intention transparent. Bajlaj Chan K’awiil’s monuments show how Dos Pilas presented its wars and lineage; the walls show that the settlement later faced danger serious enough to demand concentrated labour. Whether every defensive measure followed a particular battle remains uncertain. The evidence is strongest when it stays close to names, dates, carved figures, earthworks, ditches, and the altered pattern of occupation around them.

Cahokia leaves a different question. Its monumental centre was large, its palisades substantial, and its settlement spread across the American Bottom without preserving a dynastic inscription identifying the decisions behind construction. The mound complex at the Mississippi River site includes Monks Mound, plazas, borrow pits, and numerous smaller mounds. Its arrangement required planning and labour on a considerable scale, making a central place visible across a densely occupied landscape.

What did the palisade mean? It could indicate centralized coercion, because raising timber walls around a settlement required people to gather materials and work according to a coordinated plan. It could indicate defensive crisis, because palisades regulate movement and resist attack. It could indicate both, with a central authority able to demand labour because conflict had made the demand urgent.

The settlement distribution sharpens the question rather than settling it. Houses, activity areas, mounds, and open spaces were not arranged as though everyone lived in one compact city behind one permanent wall. Cahokia was a dispersed and changing landscape, with the monumental core connected to nearby settlements and agricultural zones. A wall around one part of that landscape might have protected an elite precinct, a ceremonial centre, a population gathered during danger, or goods and people whose value lay in their connection to the mounds.

The palisade was rebuilt or modified, and its construction seems to belong to a period when Cahokia’s political world was under pressure. That fact supports a defensive interpretation. Yet defence itself required a political decision. Someone determined where the line would run, whose labour would be summoned, which gates would be controlled, and what would be kept inside. Even if the immediate threat came from external enemies, the response could strengthen the authority of those who organized it.

Monks Mound supplies another scale of comparison. Its terraces and mass of transported earth made the central precinct unlike an ordinary residential neighbourhood. The mound complex gathered ceremony, residence, labour, and movement into a landscape where rank could be enacted through access and elevation. A person approaching the plaza encountered a built order before meeting an armed guard. The social force of the place may have rested partly in that controlled geography.

Was Cahokia ruled through fear? The mounds and palisades do not answer with a simple yes. Coercion can be present without leaving a mark on every body, and labour can be compelled through obligations that combine religious authority, kinship, reward, and threat. Impressive construction does not prove that all participants accepted the order willingly. The same project could be experienced by a leading household as honour and by a dependent labourer as a demand that could not be refused.

The question remains open because the evidence preserves structures better than decisions. Cahokia’s settlement distribution indicates a population connected to a central ceremonial complex, but it gives no transcript of commands. The palisade indicates controlled space and concern with security, but it does not identify whether the chief danger was warfare between polities, internal conflict, or a mixture that changed over time. The mound complex demonstrates organized labour and ranked access without identifying the terms under which labour was supplied. This uncertainty marks a boundary that should remain visible. Dos Pilas gives dynastic inscriptions naming rulers and victories; Tenochtitlan gives tribute records and a ritual capital whose ceremonies were described in later accounts; Cahokia gives earth, timber traces, mounds, and settlement patterns. Different evidence makes different kinds of history possible. A city without writing is not a city without politics, but its politics cannot be reconstructed by pretending that a missing inscription is present.

The palisade may have been raised because an enemy approached. It may have been raised because leaders wished to make the centre more defensible and more exclusive. It may have answered both needs at once. A threat from outside can increase demands within, while demands within can create resentment or new divisions. Cahokia’s wall belongs to the same problem encountered at Dos Pilas: the power that protects a settlement may also gather people more tightly under command.

At Cajamarca, the record suddenly gives us named men speaking and moving through an encounter, although it gives us their words through accounts written by the invaders. Francisco Pizarro had entered the Andes with a small Spanish force after years of expedition and negotiation. Atahualpa, the Inca ruler who had emerged victorious from a civil war against his brother Huáscar, was encamped near Cajamarca in 1532 with a large following. The two powers met in a political landscape already damaged by internal conflict and succession struggle.

The Spanish accounts describe the approach to Atahualpa’s camp and the effort to bring him into contact with Pizarro. Hernando Pizarro and Hernando de Soto are named among those sent towards the Inca, while the Dominican friar Vicente de Valverde appears in the accounts of the meeting itself. The narratives differ in detail and purpose, but they agree on the central sequence: Atahualpa entered Cajamarca with attendants; the Spaniards concealed much of their force around the plaza; an exchange took place; and the Spanish attacked when the encounter reached its decisive point.

The famous object in these narratives is a book or breviary offered to Atahualpa by Valverde. The accounts say that Atahualpa examined it, found no response to the spoken word expected of it, and dropped or cast it aside. Valverde then appealed to the Spaniards, and Pizarro ordered the assault. Because the episode was written by men who participated in or benefited from the conquest, the exchange cannot be repeated as though its exact words were mechanically preserved. Its function in the narratives is clear: it places a religious and legal explanation beside the violence that followed.

Atahualpa was seized amid confusion. Spanish horses, steel weapons, firearms, and disciplined movements produced effects that the Andean attendants had not encountered in this form, but the capture depended on more than technological surprise. Pizarro’s men chose a confined plaza, concealed their soldiers, and waited while Atahualpa approached under the protection of his court. They used the authority of an audience against the man who had come to conduct one.

The chroniclers describe a crush of people, the killing of attendants, and the struggle to reach Atahualpa. Pizarro himself was wounded in the hand, according to accounts that emphasize his effort to keep his soldiers from killing the Inca. Whether every detail is accurate, the event was not a formal battle in which two armies tested one another across an open field. It was a seizure carried out during a meeting, and that difference shaped its consequences.

Atahualpa’s capture disorganized the political field without destroying the administrative network that made Inca rule possible. The Spaniards held the ruler and demanded a ransom. Gold and silver were gathered from temples, storehouses, palaces, and provincial centres, then transported to Cajamarca and divided among the conquerors. The material value of the ransom drew attention, but its political significance was just as important: the Spaniards converted custody of one person into claims over the resources of an empire.

The Inca state had its own systems for moving food, textiles, labourers, and armies across difficult terrain. Roads, storehouses, provincial governors, and obligations to the ruler connected communities to Cuzco and to one another. Those systems did not cause the Spanish conquest, and the Spaniards did not invent the hierarchy they exploited. Once Atahualpa was held, however, existing channels of Inca administration helped gather the wealth demanded by his captors.

The Spanish accounts present Atahualpa as a powerful ruler defeated by providence, courage, and superior arms. They also reveal calculation. Pizarro’s force was small in relation to the population and armies of the Andes, so capturing the ruler offered a way to substitute a hostage relationship for the immediate conquest of every province. Atahualpa could issue commands from captivity, or his captors could claim that he had done so. The Spaniards needed his name because they lacked his reach.

Atahualpa attempted to manage the crisis through the ransom and through commands that the Spanish chroniclers interpreted according to their own interests. He remained a political actor in captivity, but the conditions of his action had been transformed. The man who could summon armies could no longer choose where to stand, whom to meet, or how to control the goods brought before him. His body became the place where Inca sovereignty and Spanish force were forced into an unstable relation.

The narratives then move towards execution. Atahualpa was tried and condemned in a proceeding whose charges included rebellion, idolatry, and crimes associated with the civil war. The accounts record that he was executed at Cajamarca in 1533, after baptism and strangulation by garrote rather than burning. In the narratives, the change in method followed his acceptance of baptism, though the procedure also gave a Christian form to the death of the ruler the conquerors had captured.

There is little reason to treat the trial as an independent judgment detached from Spanish power. The prisoner had been seized in an ambush-like encounter, the ransom had been extracted, and the conquerors faced the danger that his continued life might restore a centre of resistance. Legal language did not replace political calculation. It helped make the killing intelligible to the men who carried it out and defensible before authorities who might ask whether conquest had been lawful.

The Cajamarca encounter joins the earlier cases without becoming their duplicate. At Tenochtitlan, tribute and ritual made conquest recurrent and visible through a capital whose officials and priests organized goods, captives, and public meaning. At Dos Pilas, monuments and walls show a dynasty trying to hold together lineage, regional rivalry, and defence. At Cahokia, the material record leaves unresolved how centralized command and emergency protection were related. At Cajamarca, a meeting became a seizure because a small invading force used concealment, timing, weapons, and a contested claim to authority against a ruler whose own political system could still be made to work for those holding him.

The Spaniards’ victory did not prove that one people possessed a timeless appetite for violence greater than another. It emerged from a particular succession crisis, a particular expedition, a particular meeting place, and decisions made by named men. Its results were enlarged by political structures already in existence: Andean roads and storehouses, provincial officials, royal obligations, and the authority attached to the Inca person. Violence struck at the centre, then travelled outward through the channels that centre had built.

Atahualpa’s capture is often told as a contest between weapons or civilizations. The accounts show a more unsettling sequence. Pizarro promised an audience and prepared an ambush. Valverde supplied a religious frame for the encounter. Atahualpa entered with the confidence or necessity of a ruler accustomed to dealing through rank and ceremony. The plaza became a trap, and afterward the machinery of a large state helped satisfy the demands of the men who had seized its sovereign. Human beings acted with fear, ambition, obligation, calculation, and belief, while institutions gave those motives a reach that no individual body possessed.

chapters.title: Frontiers, Faiths, and Political Fragmentation
chapters.markdown:
The catalogue begins with shores, roads, walls, and harbours. Lindisfarne, an island monastery off the coast of Northumbria, entered the written record of Viking violence through the attack traditionally dated to 8 June 793. Alcuin of York, writing soon afterward, treated the assault as a calamity striking a Christian community, while the *Anglo-Saxon Chronicle* preserved the terse memory of raiders arriving after ominous signs in the sky. The monastery’s wealth was portable: vessels, precious fittings, books, and people could be seized and carried away. Its isolation reduced the number of defenders and increased the value of surprise. Men who had crossed the sea in vessels designed for speed, shallow water, and return could reach a place chosen for prayer and turn it, in a morning, into a source of captives and objects.

Viking raiding required more than a ship at the water’s edge. Crews had to be assembled, provisions secured, coasts remembered, and the gains divided when the ship returned. Agriculture set limits to the season, while tides and weather shaped the journey. A leader who brought back silver, captives, or ecclesiastical treasures could strengthen his household and attract new followers. The same maritime skill that carried a war band to Lindisfarne could carry traders to a market, settlers to a river valley, or envoys to a king. The ship widened the field of action; political relationships determined what its cargo meant.

Across the Sahara, protection gathered around a different geometry. A caravan leaving Sijilmasa or crossing toward the lands south of the desert depended first on wells and guides, then on agreements that kept travellers moving together when the horizon offered few fixed points. Maghrebi merchants and desert communities developed practices of escort, payment, warning, and retaliation around these routes. Protection could be claimed by a lineage, a local ruler, a confederation, or a group controlling access to water. A caravan’s safety rested on terms that could be renewed, broken, or enforced through the threat of violence.

Camels carried salt, cloth, metals, and other goods in trains whose length and composition changed with the route and the political climate. At Taghaza, where salt extraction supported long-distance exchange, the resource linked labourers, merchants, and armed protectors to places far beyond the mines. A convoy did not move through an empty wilderness. It passed among communities that knew the wells, the tracks, and the value of delay. A raiding party might seek animals and merchandise; a protector might demand payment for preventing that raid; a ruler might present the collection of dues as legitimate passage. The road’s commercial purpose gave armed men something to seize and gave them an argument for being paid.

Along the eastern Roman frontier, Byzantine writers used the term *akritai* for men associated with the borderlands, though the word gathered different social realities into one literary figure. In the tenth-century poems concerning Digenes Akritas, the frontier hero appears as a warrior of mixed cultural inheritance, defending the Christian Roman border while inhabiting a world of intermarriage, local rivalries, raids, and negotiated loyalties. The poem is not a payroll or census. Its value lies in showing how the frontier could be imagined: neither a clean line between two peoples nor a zone in which settled law simply ended, but a place where military service, landholding, kinship, and religious identity pressed against one another.

The Byzantine system relied on fortified places, military districts, tax obligations, local landowners, and soldiers whose service was tied to the survival of villages as well as to imperial command. At Amorion and along the Taurus approaches, walls and passes gave geography a political shape. Garrisons watched roads, messengers carried warnings, and inhabitants could be moved, recruited, taxed, or abandoned according to the fortunes of war. Arab and Byzantine forces raided across the frontier for captives, livestock, and prestige; emperors and emirs also made truces, exchanged prisoners, and arranged boundaries of use. Defense combined force with information and accommodation because the frontier could not be held by walls alone.

The ports of the Indian Ocean completed the catalogue by making rivalry mobile without requiring armies to occupy a continuous frontier. Kilwa on the East African coast, Aden at the entrance to the Red Sea, Hormuz in the Persian Gulf, and Calicut on the Malabar coast each depended on ships, pilots, customs, warehouses, credit, and rulers able to turn maritime position into revenue. Merchants carried textiles, spices, ivory, gold, horses, and other goods between regions whose political calendars did not coincide. A port’s prosperity could attract protection from a sultan and predation from a competitor.

When the Portuguese fleet commanded by Vasco da Gama reached the Malabar coast in 1498, Calicut was already a major commercial centre under the authority of the Zamorin. The Portuguese sought access to the spice trade, but they also brought armed ships and a willingness to make commerce answer to cannon. The conflict that followed involved Muslim merchants, Hindu rulers, Portuguese captains, and competing ports, each pursuing advantage through embargo, alliance, naval attack, or control of anchorage. A harbour was therefore a commercial site and a military instrument. Whoever controlled its customs house or anchorage could decide who was allowed to trade.

A raider and a soldier are often placed at opposite ends of a historical story. The raider is imagined as mobile, opportunistic, and socially loose; the soldier as settled, disciplined, and attached to a state. The cases resist that arrangement. Viking seasonal raiding needed organisation before the ship left shore and after it returned. Byzantine warfare depended on settlements that could feed, inform, and shelter fighters. Sahelian raiding operated within commercial systems that also required recognised protectors. Mobile raiding and settled warfare were connected positions within economies of force, not opposite social types.

The Viking attack on Lindisfarne is easy to detach from its setting because the episode has acquired the shape of an origin story. A fleet appears, a monastery burns, and an age of raiding seems to begin. Yet the raid was one event within a maritime world that included the North Sea, the Irish Sea, the Frankish coast, and the rivers leading into eastern Europe. Seasonal action did not mean unplanned action. Crews needed provisions, ships needed maintenance, leaders needed followers, and the people who returned with silver, captives, or ecclesiastical treasures had to decide how those gains would be divided.

The settlement of Vikings in places such as Dublin and York altered the relation between raid and rule. A town with a market and harbour could become a base from which raids were launched, a place where captives and goods were exchanged, and a centre that required defences of its own. The winter camp described in accounts of the Great Heathen Army in England was not simply a fleet pulled onto a beach. It was a place of storage, negotiation, recruitment, and political pressure. Men who raided could become rulers, while rulers could continue to raid. Residence did not end mobility; it gave mobility a more durable political base.

Byzantine frontier settlements show the reverse movement. People living near the border were not merely passive victims of armies crossing their fields. Villages, estates, forts, and market towns supplied grain, animals, labour, and intelligence. A raid could carry off inhabitants, but it could also be answered by a counter-raid from the same frontier. Military service gave some men standing and land while exposing their households to retaliation. The *akritai* of literature condensed these conditions into the figure of a heroic defender, but the practical border included farmers, tax collectors, local magnates, clergy, captives, and families divided by allegiance.

The frontier was inhabited because it was productive and strategically necessary, not because the state had solved the problem of danger. Byzantine emperors could reinforce a pass or rebuild a fort, but a defended road also directed movement and made the surrounding villages valuable to an enemy. A settlement might receive protection from Constantinople and still suffer when an army needed supplies. The fort and the farm belonged to one system, and that system distributed protection and exposure unevenly among the people who sustained it.

Sahelian caravan raiding makes the same relation visible under conditions that older European categories often obscure. A desert raider did not operate outside commerce as its pure enemy. The raider understood the value of the route because the route carried wealth. A group that attacked caravans could later bargain for protection, settle near a water source, or use political alliances to make its demands regular. Merchants, pastoralists, rulers, and armed escorts could change places across a lifetime. Their conduct depended on access to animals, wells, information, and patrons.

Accounts of trans-Saharan trade often emphasise exchange and the spread of Islam, while accounts of raiding emphasise predation. Neither alone describes the route from Sijilmasa toward the Niger bend. Payment for safe passage could be understood as a customary due by one party and as extortion by another. A ruler who punished raiders might be defending merchants, asserting control over a tax base, or competing with a neighbouring ruler for the same traffic. Violence entered the price of movement through political decisions about who could charge, who could protect, and whose claim would be enforced.

The temptation to divide societies into raiding peoples and peaceful peoples comes partly from the language of sources. A monastery records an attack; a court chronicle records a campaign; a merchant describes a dangerous road. Each record selects a crisis and gives it a moral vocabulary. The Viking is made barbarous, the frontier warrior loyal, the caravan protector necessary, and the port ruler commercial or tyrannical according to the author’s position. Those judgements are evidence of political meaning, but they are not neutral descriptions of whole populations.

Economic pressure alone does not explain the pattern. Scarcity could make animals, land, or trade more valuable, but whether scarcity produced migration, bargaining, raiding, taxation, or war depended on who could command men and define a lawful claim. Technology widened reach: the longship moved quickly along coasts and rivers, while the camel made desert traffic possible. Neither device supplied a motive by itself. Leaders, households, merchants, and states made each technology dangerous by attaching rewards and obligations to its use.

The First Crusade carried these entanglements into the eastern Mediterranean, where religious promises, princely ambition, commercial calculation, and military necessity became inseparable in the aftermath of conquest. Jerusalem in 1099 was not only a sacred destination. It was a city with neighbourhoods, markets, water systems, workshops, religious institutions, and inhabitants whose lives were reorganised by the arrival of an army claiming divine sanction.

When the crusading army entered Jerusalem in July 1099, the surviving accounts describe a siege followed by the capture of the city and extensive killing. Latin authors such as Raymond of Aguilers presented the event as a victory granted to the crusaders, and their descriptions of bloodshed helped turn the capture into a sign of divine favour. Muslim and Jewish communities experienced the conquest as dispossession and death. The Latin army’s assault passed through walls and streets, but its consequences reached households that had not chosen the expedition and could not negotiate with the men who claimed the city.

The names most often attached to the conquest are Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Tancred, and Robert of Normandy. Behind them stood men who had travelled from different regions of Europe, joined for different reasons, and expected different rewards. Some sought remission of sins, some land or status, some protection for fellow pilgrims, and some the chance to profit from conquest. A single religious banner gathered those motives without making them identical. Once Jerusalem was taken, the language of pilgrimage had to coexist with the work of governing a populated city.

The new rulers distributed property, installed Latin clergy, and defended the territory against surrounding powers. The Holy Sepulchre became a centre of Christian kingship as well as devotion. Jerusalem’s Muslim and Jewish inhabitants were killed, expelled, or subjected to new conditions, while Christian communities of different rites negotiated their place under Latin rule. Conquest did not simply replace one administration with another. It altered access to homes, markets, shrines, and protection, and gave violence an institutional form that continued after the army’s departure.

News of Jerusalem moved outward through letters, sermons, oral reports, and returning participants. For those who had not seen the city, the event could be remembered as a miracle, a massacre, a warning, or proof that enemies had been defeated. Such memories affected recruitment and resistance. A city’s capture became an argument used in later campaigns, while people displaced by it carried knowledge of Latin methods and intentions to other towns. Armies moved through the Levant, but the meaning of their violence travelled through stories.

Antioch revealed a different difficulty. The city was captured in June 1098 after a long siege marked by hunger, disease, desertion, negotiation, and assault. Bohemond of Taranto, Raymond of Saint-Gilles, and other leaders had entered the expedition with shared enemies but competing plans. Once Antioch fell, Bohemond claimed the city, while other leaders argued over promises, leadership, and the obligation to continue towards Jerusalem. The conquest created a prize whose possession threatened to divide the coalition that had won it.

Antioch’s population had already lived through the turbulence of Seljuk expansion, Byzantine recovery, local rule, and the arrival of the crusaders. The citadel, walls, gates, markets, and surrounding agricultural land gave the city a value no devotional description could exhaust. Control of Antioch meant access to routes between Anatolia and Syria, to the Orontes valley, and to a port at Saint Symeon. A lord who held it could tax movement and withstand attack. A population that survived the siege found itself inside a new political experiment whose rulers needed both revenue and allies.

The crusaders’ victory at Antioch did not end danger. Kerbogha of Mosul arrived with a large army, and the crusaders, still divided and weakened, faced encirclement inside the city. The discovery of the Holy Lance, described by Raymond of Aguilers and others, helped generate the religious confidence needed for the army’s sortie and victory in June 1098. Hunger made action necessary; belief helped make a risky action acceptable and coordinated. Material desperation and sacred interpretation worked together in the decision to fight.

Afterward, Bohemond remained in Antioch, while other leaders continued south. The principality that developed there depended on fortresses, tribute, alliances, local administrators, military households, and relations with Armenian and Syrian Christian communities. Latin rulers could offer protection against one enemy while imposing new burdens or provoking another. Christians who had suffered under previous regimes did not thereby become a single political community with the conquerors. Religious affinity could assist negotiation, but it did not erase differences of rite, language, rank, or interest.

The displaced communities of the Levant carried the aftermath beyond the captured cities. Some inhabitants fled before or during sieges; others were expelled, enslaved, or moved through military and commercial networks. Captives taken in Jerusalem, Antioch, and later campaigns could be sold, exchanged, ransomed, or retained as labourers. Families were separated along the same routes that carried grain, letters, and troops. A community displaced from a city did not vanish from history, but the sources often record its absence more clearly than its later life. Those who remained had to deal with altered taxes, courts, landholding, and armed protection. A village near Jerusalem might supply food to the new kingdom and fear raids from neighbouring Muslim powers. A Christian community near Antioch might gain room to worship under one ruler and lose influence under another. Jewish survivors and refugees entered other towns or joined networks of trade and kinship. “The inhabitants” hides these differences, just as “the crusaders” hides the disputes among the men who claimed the conquest.

The aftermath changed the surrounding political field. Muslim rulers in Damascus, Aleppo, Mosul, and Egypt confronted Latin enclaves that had not existed before the expedition. Their responses combined military resistance with negotiation, rivalry, and the search for allies. Zengi’s capture of Edessa in 1144 later became a powerful symbol in Latin Europe, while Nur al-Din and Saladin built authority partly through the promise of opposing the crusader states. The violence of 1099 supplied political language to rulers who came after it.

Saladin’s entry into Jerusalem in October 1187, after the battle of Hattin, was shaped by the memory of the earlier massacre. The surrender arrangements allowed many inhabitants to leave through ransom or payment, though the process was unequal and not everyone escaped easily. Latin churches were converted or reassigned, while some Christian shrines and communities were accommodated. The contrast with 1099 mattered to Muslim and Christian writers, but it should not be turned into a simple proof of moral progress. Saladin was managing legitimacy, prisoners, property, and the response of a city whose capture had strategic as well as religious value.

The people of Jerusalem experienced conquest as a change in the terms under which ordinary actions were possible. Who could open a shop, hold land, cross a gate, worship in a shrine, or claim the protection of a judge depended on the ruler of the moment. The First Crusade attached violence to new titles, new settlements, and new claims about rightful possession. A sacred destination became a capital, and the capital became a prize in arguments that continued long after the first army departed.

Among the most searching documents from the later crisis of Islamic political order is a fatwa associated with Ibn Taymiyya and the Mongol rulers who had entered the lands of the Abbasid caliphate. Ibn Taymiyya, a scholar from Damascus who died in 1328, addressed a problem that military victory alone could not settle: how should Muslims judge rulers who professed Islam but continued to govern according to the *yasa*, the law attributed to Chinggis Khan, and who attacked Muslim territories?

The document’s force lies in its conditional structure. Ibn Taymiyya did not treat political violence as legitimate merely because an enemy had been defeated or because a ruler claimed the Muslim name. He examined conduct, law, allegiance, and the relation between profession and rule. The Mongols had converted in significant numbers, and some Mongol leaders presented themselves as Muslims. Their armies nevertheless invaded Syria, threatened Damascus, and maintained political practices that Ibn Taymiyya regarded as incompatible with the obligations of Islamic governance. His argument turned on legitimate authority. A ruler was not made rightful by genealogy, military success, or a public declaration alone. Rule required obedience to the law of Islam and protection of the Muslim community. When a regime claimed Islam while judging by another code and warring against Muslims, Ibn Taymiyya could classify it as an enemy requiring resistance. The category did not depend on the ruler’s ancestry. It depended on the relation between belief, law, and political action. This was dangerous language because it could direct violence inward. The Mongol rulers were no longer simply outsiders beyond the religious community. Their partial adoption of Islam made the question sharper: could a ruler be treated as an unbeliever, or as an illegitimate aggressor, when he professed the faith but violated its political obligations? Ibn Taymiyya’s response gave legal and theological form to the judgement that profession without lawful conduct was insufficient. His text made authority answerable to a standard higher than the ruler’s declaration.

“Profession without lawful conduct was insufficient.”

The fatwa should be read alongside the circumstances in which it was produced. Damascus was not a schoolroom detached from war. The Mongol invasions had displaced populations, damaged towns, and placed scholars and rulers under pressure. Ibn Taymiyya participated in the public debates of his time and urged resistance. The document’s religious reasoning was therefore also a response to an immediate political emergency, though it cannot be reduced to personal anger or patriotic speech. Its terms connected battlefield decisions to a jurisprudential argument about the obligations of rulers and subjects.

The earlier frontier cases clarify the stakes. The Byzantine *akritai* represented defence at a border where identities overlapped, while Ibn Taymiyya confronted a regime whose religious identity was disputed from within the community it ruled. In both cases, authority was tested by conduct under pressure. A wall, a military title, or a profession of faith did not settle who could command obedience. The question was whether protection, law, and allegiance were joined in a manner recognised as legitimate.

Ibn Taymiyya’s use of precedent and legal reasoning also constrained the violence he could justify. He was not writing that every political disagreement permitted killing. He distinguished among enemies and considered the consequences of fighting them. The Mongols’ actions, their laws, and their attacks on Muslim lands supplied the grounds for resistance. Religious vocabulary sharpened political conflict through categories, conditions, and inherited arguments rather than through an undifferentiated call to rage.

The document records a struggle over names. “Muslim,” “Mongol,” “ruler,” “enemy,” and “legitimate authority” were not neutral descriptions; each carried consequences for obedience, war, and punishment. A community could be urged to resist a ruler because resistance was presented as a duty when rule had broken its lawful purpose. The same vocabulary could narrow the space for compromise. Once an opponent was placed outside legitimate authority, negotiation became more difficult and coercion easier to defend. Yet the Mongol world did not divide neatly between faith and force. Mongol rulers governed Muslim cities through officials, tax collectors, military commanders, and local notables. Muslim scholars served under rulers they disliked or criticised. Merchants continued to seek profit across boundaries that armies treated as hostile. A ruler might be condemned in a fatwa and still be encountered in a market, a treaty, a tax office, or a diplomatic mission.

The fatwa belongs to the history of aggression as a close record of how religious judgement can organise political action. It supplied a vocabulary through which a community could identify unlawful rule, distinguish nominal affiliation from legitimate conduct, and authorise resistance. That vocabulary addressed Mongol armies, Syrian towns, displaced people, and the threatened authority of local rulers. Belief gave the conflict a moral shape; institutions and armies gave the shape force.

chapters.title: Steppe Powers and Connected Worlds
chapters.markdown:
The Mongol armies entered a political field that settled rulers often described too simply. To call the steppe a place of raiders was to miss the work required to make mobile power durable: households had to attach themselves to leaders, pasture had to be allocated, fighting men counted, and victory converted into obligations that survived a season’s movement. *The Secret History of the Mongols* begins not with an empire already formed but with a child whose position is repeatedly made insecure by decisions made around him.

Temüjin was born, according to the *Secret History*, while his father Yesügei was returning from a raid against the Tatars. The child was said to have arrived with a clot of blood in his hand, a sign that marks his future connection with killing and rule. The surrounding details are less ornamental. Yesügei arranged Temüjin’s betrothal to Börte of the Onggirat while the boy was still young, then was poisoned by Tatars before he could secure his family’s place among the tribes. Temüjin’s mother, Hö’elün, was left with children and dependants whom the Tayichi’ut abandoned beside the Onon River.

The family survived by gathering roots, catching fish, and hunting small animals. The *Secret History* gives these hardships a domestic scale: the children disputed over food, Bö’orchu joined Temüjin after finding one of his stolen horses, and Jamuqa became first a sworn companion and later an enemy. A horse could be taken; a marriage could be broken; brothers could become rivals over a marmot or a fish. The narrative does not describe an abstract “Mongol character.” It follows a household whose prospects depended on kin, livestock, marriage ties, and the willingness of stronger men to recognize its claims.

Temüjin’s first important acts were acts of attachment. He sought the protection of Toghoril, the Kerait ruler known in the *Secret History* as Ong Khan, renewing the alliance formed through his father’s earlier relationship with him. After Börte was abducted by the Merkit, Temüjin called on Toghoril and Jamuqa for help. The rescue was a military action, but the marriage became politically useful because Börte belonged to the Onggirat and because the alliance gathered men connected by obligation rather than by a single settled territory. A household joined a larger coalition; the coalition gained a cause and a marriage; its leader could demonstrate authority through distribution.

Jamuqa’s friendship with Temüjin developed into formal unions, and the *Secret History* presents their separation as a question of political style. Some men preferred Jamuqa’s established rank and ceremonial precedence. Others moved toward Temüjin because he promoted followers according to service and loyalty rather than preserving every privilege of lineage. The account may be shaped by the victorious ruler’s memory, but it repeatedly returns to named followers and particular rewards. Jelme, Subedei, Muqali, and Bo’orchu appear not as interchangeable instruments but as men whose careers became evidence for the coalition Temüjin was building. He punished betrayal with unusual severity.
