Scarcity alone does not select a neighbour for deportation or make a city’s evacuation compulsory.

Technology altered reach without dictating purpose. Trains allowed the Nazi regime to coordinate deportations across occupied Europe, but railway lines did not decide that Jews should be killed. Cambodia’s roads, radios, weapons, and administrative communications helped the Khmer Rouge move orders and people, but they did not generate the doctrine of revolutionary purification. In both cases, violence required people who interpreted instructions, produced records, guarded roads, allocated food, and converted general ideology into local action. Some obeyed from conviction, some from fear, some for advantage, and some resisted in limited ways. The surviving evidence does not permit one motive to be assigned to all participants.

The difference between the cases is therefore political and institutional. The Nazi genocide was organized around the destruction of Jews as a racialized people across a European sphere of conquest, with killing becoming the central objective of deportation. Khmer Rouge violence sought to reconstruct Cambodia through the destruction of social categories and the submission of the population to revolutionary labour and surveillance, while also targeting ethnic and religious groups. Both show how political ideas can turn administration into persecution. “Genocide” must be used with attention to the group named by the perpetrators, the reach of their policy, and the means by which destruction was pursued.

A document from a villa beside Berlin’s Wannsee lake has often been made to carry more weight than its pages can bear. The Wannsee Protocol records a meeting held on 20 January 1942, chaired by Reinhard Heydrich, with Adolf Eichmann preparing the document. The participants were senior officials from the SS, the security police, the Foreign Ministry, the Justice Ministry, the Interior Ministry, the Party Chancellery, the General Government, and the administration of the occupied eastern territories. Their titles mattered because the meeting concerned the coordination of work already spread across offices.

Heydrich’s opening claim was that Hermann Göring had appointed him to prepare a solution to the “Jewish question” in Europe and direct the work of a central office. The protocol refers to the earlier emigration policy, describes the German shift toward evacuation to the east, and presents a projected population of more than eleven million Jews in Europe. The figures include countries under German control, allied states, occupied territories, and places whose inclusion depended on political definitions of Jewish identity. The number is an administrative total, assembled so that a policy can be imagined at a continental scale.

The prose then turns to the mixed categories created by racial law. It discusses “Mischlinge,” intermarried people, and whether those classified as partly Jewish should be sterilized, exempted, or treated as Jews. The language is cold because its work is classificatory. A person’s fate is made to depend on grandparents, marriage, descent, and the status assigned by the state. The meeting did not discover these categories. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and later decrees had already created the legal distinctions. At Wannsee, officials considered how those distinctions would be handled within a more radical policy.

Several passages describe deported Jews being put to work in the east. The wording refers to a process in which those fit for labour would be separated from those unable to work and in which “natural diminution” would occur among the weaker. The euphemism places killing inside a sequence of labour, exhaustion, selection, and disappearance. The protocol also speaks of treatment of the surviving remnant, whose members would have to be dealt with appropriately because their release or survival might lead to renewed Jewish life. Its language points toward exterminatory intent through bureaucratic indirection. Yet Wannsee was not the first decision to murder Europe’s Jews, nor was it a command signed there to begin the Holocaust. Mass shootings had already occurred behind the eastern front after the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. Killing centres had begun to operate or were being prepared. Deportations and ghetto clearances were already under way. Heydrich’s meeting gathered officials whose departments had different responsibilities and required them to accept SS direction of the European policy. The protocol records coordination inside an existing campaign.

The participants’ administrative roles reveal the meeting’s practical character. Wilhelm Stuckart represented the Interior Ministry, where racial definitions had been drafted and applied. State Secretary Martin Luther attended for the Foreign Ministry, which had to pressure allied and occupied governments and manage international consequences. Josef Bühler came from the administration of the General Government in occupied Poland, where ghettos, starvation, forced labour, and mass killing were already transforming the lives of Polish Jews. Rudolf Lange represented the security police in the occupied Baltic region, where he had been involved in mass shootings. Georg Leibbrandt attended from the Reich Ministry for the Occupied Eastern Territories. Their presence connected legal classification, diplomacy, occupation government, policing, and territorial administration.

Eichmann’s role was equally revealing. He was not the supreme author of the policy, but he organized the meeting, prepared the text, and worked on Jewish affairs within the Reich Security Main Office. His office dealt with deportation plans, population figures, correspondence, and the movement of people into ghettos and killing sites. Administrative labour did not stand outside the crime. It enabled the crime to be distributed across departments so that few participants needed to describe the whole process in a single sentence.

The surviving protocol is a copy, not a verbatim transcript. Its polished wording reflects the conventions of a record designed for officials. It omits the bluntest language associated with the spoken discussion, and its euphemisms require comparison with deportation orders, railway records, killing reports, camp records, and testimony. The document shows officials being brought into a common framework under Heydrich’s authority. It shows the geographic scope of the intended policy and the legal problems that Nazi administrators expected to solve. It also shows how destruction could be made to look like a problem of jurisdiction and paperwork.

The villa meeting belongs to the same history as the railway timetable, but it should not be mistaken for the timetable’s origin. The protocol is valuable because it catches the state’s offices speaking to one another while murder was being standardized. Categories, territories, and responsibilities are joined on the page. The people discussed are converted into columns and subcategories, the departments that will act are placed in relation to one another, and the future is described as an administrative task. Its force lies in that ordinariness. No theatrical declaration was needed in the record. Heydrich could cite Göring’s authority, Eichmann could prepare population figures, and representatives of ministries could discuss mixed marriages while killing operations expanded elsewhere. The document preserves the grammar by which a government turns an ideological enemy into a transport problem, a labour calculation, a diplomatic request, and a question of legal definition. The destruction of European Jews did not depend on one paper alone; it depended on decisions made by people who held particular offices and used them to move a policy through the world.

chapters.title: After 1945: Deterrence, Insurgency, and Uneven Decline
chapters.markdown:
The postwar world contained several kinds of organised violence at once: the nuclear standoff, in which the United States and Soviet Union prepared for a war neither could safely begin; the proxy war, in which outside powers supplied weapons, advisers, money, and diplomatic cover to local combatants; the decolonisation campaign, in which imperial governments defended territorial claims and anticolonial movements sought sovereignty; the insurgency and counterinsurgency, in which armed movements and governments fought over administration and allegiance; and peacekeeping, in which an international force attempted to keep separated enemies from returning to open war. These forms overlapped without becoming identical. In October 1962, the Cuban Missile Crisis joined a nuclear standoff to a contest over geography, credibility, and the political meaning of an American quarantine around Cuba. John F. Kennedy and Nikita Khrushchev exchanged messages while naval vessels, missiles, aircraft, and military commands placed decisions beyond the reach of any single conversation. The crisis ended through negotiation, including the withdrawal of Soviet missiles from Cuba and the later removal of American Jupiter missiles from Turkey. Its danger came from the attachment of local territory to the survival claims of two global powers.

Angola supplied a different pattern. After Portuguese rule ended in 1975, the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, and the National Front for the Liberation of Angola fought for control of the new state. Cuba sent troops in support of the MPLA, while South Africa intervened militarily and the United States and Soviet Union supported opposing sides through changing channels. The Angolan Civil War endured because domestic rivals were connected to external resources. Oil and diamonds helped sustain the struggle, while foreign arms and recognition gave competing governments reasons to continue. A civil war became an international contest without ceasing to be a fight over Angola’s presidency, territory, and political order.

From 1954 to 1962, the Algerian War joined anticolonial nationalism to an elaborate system of surveillance and punishment. The Front de Libération Nationale sought independence from France; the French army and police sought to preserve French rule. Bombings in Algiers and attacks in the countryside were answered by arrests, torture, executions, and the movement of civilians through controlled zones. Each side presented violence as evidence of a larger right to govern. French settlers, Algerian Muslims, soldiers, urban workers, rural communities, and political prisoners occupied different positions within that struggle. “Algerian” concealed divisions that the war made dangerous, while “French” included officials, conscripts, settlers, and opponents of the colonial system.

Beginning in 1948, the Malayan Emergency displayed the counterinsurgent form with unusual clarity. The British confronted the Malayan Communist Party and its armed wing in a landscape where rubber estates and tin mines depended on the security of villages, forest tracks, and supply routes. British intelligence sought information from informers, captured documents, patrols, and questioning. The Briggs Plan, associated with Lieutenant-General Harold Briggs, relocated many rural Chinese squatters into guarded “New Villages,” restricting the flow of food and recruits to guerrillas in the jungle. The policy reduced insurgent access to supplies, but it also subjected civilians to surveillance and coercion. In Malaya, a food ration and a gate could serve the same campaign as a rifle.

Cyprus offered a slower and more limited form of international restraint. After violence between Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities and the breakdown of constitutional government, the United Nations established a peacekeeping operation in 1964. The United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus remained between opposing communities along a buffer zone that later became known as the Green Line. Soldiers patrolled, observed, reported, and helped prevent local incidents from becoming renewed large-scale fighting. They did not settle the political dispute.

A force created to hold separation in place could reduce immediate violence while leaving its causes unresolved. The Cuban crisis threatened destruction through the decisions of governments with enormous arsenals. Angola prolonged violence through external sponsorship of local armies and movements. Algeria placed a colonial population under pressure from a struggle over sovereignty, while Malaya made intelligence and food central to the defeat of an insurgency. Cyprus showed how an international presence could restrain armed actors without producing agreement.

A confident account of the period can be built from a reasonable observation: nuclear deterrence discouraged the United States and Soviet Union from fighting one another directly, the Geneva Conventions after 1949 strengthened rules for the treatment of prisoners and civilians, and the long-term trend in interstate war appears to have declined. From these facts comes the argument that the postwar world became steadily safer through fear, law, and international institutions.

Nuclear deterrence theory rests on a severe calculation. If two states possess secure retaliatory forces, neither can attack without risking unacceptable destruction. The expected cost of aggression becomes greater than the expected political gain. Leaders must believe that an opponent can survive a first strike, that retaliation will follow, and that the threat is credible enough to shape conduct before a crisis begins. Peace between major powers may then rest not on trust but on the knowledge that victory cannot protect either side from the consequences of war.

The Cuban Missile Crisis supports part of this argument. Kennedy and Khrushchev had reasons to avoid escalation, and nuclear weapons made their choices more dangerous than a conventional dispute over a naval blockade. The crisis ended without a superpower war. Deterrence, however, did not remove aggression from the international system. It redirected competition toward Cuba, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Angola, the Middle East, Central America, covert action, arms transfers, and support for governments or movements whose own populations carried the cost.

Angola shows the division clearly. The Soviet Union and the United States avoided a direct battlefield confrontation, but their restraint did not protect Angolan civilians from a war extended by foreign resources. Cuba’s military intervention and South Africa’s operations gave the conflict a regional and global dimension. A stable nuclear balance at the top could coexist with instability below it. Security for states capable of destroying one another did not provide security for every society drawn into their rivalry.

International law made a genuine difference, though law worked through enforcement, expectation, documentation, and political pressure rather than by removing the motives for violence. The Geneva Conventions of 1949 revised and expanded protections for wounded soldiers, prisoners of war, and civilians. Common Article 3 established minimum standards for conflicts not of an international character. Those rules gave governments, courts, humanitarian organisations, and witnesses a language with which to identify abuse. They also marked some acts as crimes even when commanders described them as necessities.

The Algerian War demonstrates both the reach and weakness of such rules. France had courts, ministries, military regulations, and a public language of legality, yet torture and collective punishment became associated with the struggle against the FLN. The existence of law did not prevent officials from narrowing the category of protected person or presenting coercion as emergency security. In Malaya, the British used detention, restrictions, resettlement, and food controls while describing the campaign as a struggle to restore order. Legal language could constrain conduct, but it could also organise legitimacy around a war.

Postwar interstate-war data support a narrower conclusion than steady moral improvement. Major wars between states became less frequent after 1945 than in the first half of the twentieth century, and the absence of direct war between the United States and Soviet Union is historically important. Yet counts depend on definitions. A war may be counted by battle deaths, duration, participating states, or whether an intervention is classified as interstate, civil, or internationalised. Data focused on battlefield deaths may omit displacement, famine, imprisonment, sexual violence, disease, and the destruction of homes and livelihoods. A decline in one measure can coexist with persistence or growth in another.

The postwar record shows restraint and danger together. The United Nations created procedures for mediation, sanctions, observation, and peacekeeping. The law of armed conflict supplied standards that activists and institutions could invoke. Nuclear weapons made direct war between great powers terrifyingly costly. None of these developments guaranteed a steady decline in human harm. They altered the calculations through which governments justified, concealed, and sometimes limited violence.

The safer-world argument becomes persuasive when stated precisely: interstate war among the most powerful states declined, and rules against certain abuses became more explicit and influential. It becomes too broad when civil wars, colonial campaigns, proxy interventions, and civilian suffering are treated as secondary evidence. Cyprus shows how patrols and separation reduced immediate clashes without solving the political conflict. The nuclear standoff shows that leaders stepped back from escalation without producing a general peace.

External sponsorship altered civil wars first by changing what local combatants could possess. A movement with rifles, food, radios, and medical supplies could hold ground longer than one dependent on captured weapons. A government with helicopters and advisers could survive defeats that might otherwise have forced negotiation. Sponsorship also changed political time. Leaders dependent on a local tax base or village support had to consider exhaustion close to home; leaders supplied from abroad could continue after the population had been depleted.

United States support in Afghanistan illustrates the chain. After the Soviet intervention of December 1979, Washington supported Afghan resistance forces through Pakistan. Weapons and money moved through a system in which American decisions, Pakistani intelligence, Afghan commanders, religious networks, transporters, and local communities occupied different places. The Stinger missile, supplied to mujahideen forces in the 1980s, altered the danger faced by Soviet aircraft and helicopters. A weapon designed and manufactured far from Afghanistan affected the balance of a war through intermediaries who pursued their own political goals.

Pakistan’s Afghan frontier provided more than a route. The borderlands contained refugee populations, religious schools, trading networks, tribal authorities, armed groups, and areas where central governments exercised uneven control. Safe havens allowed fighters to withdraw, recruit, train, store supplies, and return across the frontier. A government pursuing insurgents inside Afghanistan could not easily strike every base without risking confrontation with Pakistan. Defeat in one valley therefore did not necessarily mean destruction of the organisation. Men and equipment could move beyond the immediate reach of the opposing army, and the fight could begin again from another side of the border.

Soviet support in Angola worked through a different distance. Moscow supplied weapons and military assistance to the MPLA government, while Cuban forces provided the large external military presence that helped defend it. The Soviet Union did not simply command every Angolan operation. Angolan commanders, Cuban officers, South African forces, UNITA leaders, and American officials made decisions within a conflict shaped by foreign aid. Weapons strengthened the government while reducing its need to compromise, especially when supplies allowed battlefield survival to appear as evidence that political victory remained possible.

Intelligence changed the war before a shot was fired. In Malaya, British officials needed to know who carried messages, who brought rice into the forest, which paths were used at night, and which villagers feared the guerrillas more than the security forces. Information could come from a captured letter, an informer, an interrogation, a patrol report, or an officer who understood the local geography. Each item required interpretation. A name in a notebook became useful only when officials connected it to a person, a household, a route, and a decision about what to do next.

The Briggs Plan attempted to make that information more reliable by concentrating rural Chinese squatters in New Villages. Barbed wire, identity checks, curfews, food distribution, and controlled gates placed civilian life inside a system designed to separate the population from the insurgency. The British could monitor who entered and left, calculate food needs, and make unregistered movement suspicious. Residents, meanwhile, bore the burden of a war they had not chosen. Protection and compulsion occupied the same settlement.

Counterinsurgency therefore worked through a sequence that was military, administrative, and political. Officials identified a population considered connected to the insurgency. They restricted movement and supplies, gathered information through patrols and informers, and used it to arrest, persuade, relocate, or attack. They offered roads, schools, land guarantees, wages, or political concessions where these might weaken insurgent appeal. The government then measured success by reduced attacks and improved control, although civilians could experience the same policy as security in one week and intimidation in the next.

The Afghan case shows why no such sequence was automatic. Foreign support increased the insurgents’ ability to fight, but it did not create unity among them. Commanders competed over territory, resources, prestige, and religious or political authority. The Pakistani frontier protected some networks while exposing others to dependence on Pakistani decisions. American aid weakened Soviet forces and the Kabul government, yet the end of one foreign occupation did not settle who should rule Afghanistan. Sponsorship could end one balance and leave several armed claimants in place.

Angola likewise remained more than a superpower chessboard. Oil revenues and diamond extraction shaped the resources available to the contenders, while regional loyalties and state offices shaped how those resources were used. Foreign patrons supplied means, but local leaders decided how to use them against rivals and communities. Outside resources entered existing struggles over land, office, and belonging. New technology enlarged the reach of the struggle; it did not erase its local meaning.

A peace agreement becomes possible when the costs of continued war alter the calculations of people who can command armed followers. In El Salvador, negotiations between the government and the Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front unfolded through international mediation and prolonged contact rather than through one sudden conversion to trust. The war had begun in a setting of political exclusion, repression, social inequality, and armed opposition. By the early 1990s, military force had not produced a decisive victory, and the collapse of the Cold War reduced the external setting that had helped sustain the conflict.

The negotiations recorded in the United Nations process moved through questions that could not be separated neatly. The FMLN sought political participation and guarantees that an armed movement would not simply disarm into vulnerability. The government and armed forces faced demands concerning human rights, the military’s political role, policing, and accountability. Elections could not settle these questions by themselves, because an election held under the old security structure might leave the sources of fear untouched. Disarmament required confidence; confidence required institutional change.

The United Nations Truth Commission later described patterns of abuses during the Salvadoran conflict, including killings, disappearances, and attacks associated with state forces, death squads, and the FMLN. Its work gave the negotiations a documented human context: named victims, identified institutions, and findings about responsibility replaced the convenient fiction that violence had been an undifferentiated eruption by both sides. The commission’s report, *From Madness to Hope*, did not make every case equally clear, but it connected the political settlement to people whose lives had been treated as instruments of war.

At Chapultepec Castle in Mexico City, on 16 January 1992, the parties signed the Chapultepec Peace Accords. The signing marked the end of twelve years of civil war and set out changes to the armed forces, the creation of a new civilian police force, electoral and judicial reforms, and the demobilisation and incorporation of former combatants into political life. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali represented the United Nations, whose mediation and verification had helped carry the agreement from negotiation into implementation.

The ceremony was a political act, but the agreement mattered because it described procedures. The armed forces were to withdraw from political policing and accept a revised role. The National Civilian Police was to be separate from the military and include personnel drawn from the former opposition as well as existing security structures. The FMLN was to disarm, demobilise, and become a legal political party. Land, elections, human rights, and judicial questions entered the same settlement because the war had made each of them part of the problem of authority.

The public record of the signing preserves the names of the principal representatives and the terms they accepted. It gives less access to the private fears carried by ordinary combatants, relatives of the disappeared, displaced families, and communities that had learned to survive between armies. That gap should remain a gap. The source records the agreement, its institutional reforms, and the international role; it does not permit an account of what every Salvadoran felt as weapons were surrendered.

Implementation took time and did not make the country peaceful in every sense. A civil war can end while violence persists through crime, inequality, political intimidation, or weak courts. The accords changed the relation between armed force and electoral competition, but they could not restore those killed or erase habits formed under war. Their achievement was specific: they moved the principal struggle for national power from armies toward parties, police, courts, elections, and public argument.

The path from the Cuban Missile Crisis to Chapultepec passes through no simple ascent. Nuclear weapons restrained direct conflict among superpowers while proxy wars enlarged local suffering. International law defined protections while governments violated them or narrowed their application. Intelligence and resettlement could defeat an insurgency while placing civilians under coercive control. A peacekeeping force could hold a line for decades; a peace agreement could replace armies with institutions only when combatants accepted that survival required a political settlement.

Human aggressiveness remained present in the postwar world, but its scale and direction followed the channels built around it. Missiles made a crisis global in minutes. Radios, aircraft, and foreign weapons connected remote battlefields to distant capitals. Borders offered sanctuary as well as division. Ministries classified populations, distributed rations, and gathered intelligence. Courts and treaties offered restraints that were imperfect but usable. In El Salvador, negotiation gave armed rivals a way to seek power without making the country itself the battlefield. The decline was real where it occurred, but it was uneven, negotiated, and dependent on choices made by particular governments, commanders, diplomats, and citizens.

chapters.title: What History Can and Cannot Explain
chapters.markdown:
In Kigali, the crisis did not arrive as a single order travelling cleanly from a government office to every road and household. It gathered through meetings, radio messages, guarded buildings, hurried departures, and decisions made by men who understood that authority was changing hands. On 6 April 1994, the aircraft carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down as it approached the capital. His death opened a struggle over who could command the army, the administration, the radio, and the streets. The interim government that followed did not merely inherit confusion. It worked through officials, soldiers, local administrators, and political networks that defined enemies and demanded obedience, while the Rwandan Patriotic Front advanced from the north and fighting spread through the country.

Government statements and administrative traces show ministers and senior officials attempting to preserve a state under conditions of collapse. Their language of emergency quickly joined a language of ethnic threat. Kigali’s roadblocks made that change visible. Men stopped vehicles and pedestrians, demanded identity papers, and searched for Tutsi. They questioned people about their neighbourhoods, names, and affiliations. The barrier itself might be improvised from timber or stones, but it connected the capital’s streets to the larger political decision that a person’s identity could determine whether he or she was permitted to pass. The paper or answer presented there mattered because armed men had been given, or had claimed, the right to interpret it.

Some officials summoned residents, distributed instructions, or encouraged patrols. Soldiers guarded intersections. Civilians joined armed groups, carried lists, pointed out houses, or participated in assaults. Other civilians hid neighbours, offered false explanations at a barrier, opened churches or compounds, or tried to move relatives towards places they believed safer. The surviving accounts do not turn Kigali into a city in which everyone chose the same side. They show fear and coercion changing the cost of refusal. An ordinary act of recognition—knowing a name, a face, or a family—could become assistance to persecution, while a false answer could become an attempt to save a life.

The evidence from Kigali is uneven, and its unevenness should remain visible. Government statements and administrative traces preserve the vocabulary of order, defence, and loyalty. Survivor testimony preserves what those words could mean at a barrier or inside a threatened neighbourhood. A proclamation may show what officials wanted heard; a survivor’s account may preserve the sequence of an encounter, the clothing of a person who intervened, or the words spoken before a gate was opened. These records do not describe the same moment from the same position. Reading them together does not make either complete. It lets the historian place official intention beside lived consequence without mistaking one for the other.

At Kibuye, on the western shore of Lake Kivu, survivor testimony recalls people gathering in churches, schools, stadiums, and other places where the presence of many seemed to offer protection. That hope was repeatedly disappointed. Accounts describe crowds driven from one refuge to another, attackers arriving with weapons, and the separation of those who could flee from those who could not. The testimony is personal and local: a relative recognised among the dead, a route taken through a familiar settlement, a hiding place entered or betrayed, an official whose words gave assurance before violence began. The accounts place public authority and local knowledge inside the experience of a person trying to survive. A refuge was also a place that could be searched; a familiar road could become a route of flight or capture.

At Kibuye, as in Kigali, an official’s presence could mean protection or danger. A prefect, burgomaster, soldier, or local notable did not possess the same reach, yet each could affect whether people were assembled or dispersed, sheltered or handed over. The interim government’s crisis was therefore also a crisis of delegated rule. Orders did not need to be obeyed everywhere in identical form to produce widespread harm. They needed to make certain actions legitimate, identify a group as a danger, and give local actors reason to believe that participation would be rewarded or refusal punished.

The testimony from Kibuye records survival after the fact. It does not let us enter every mind before every choice. It does show the material pressures under which choices were made: blocked roads, crowded refuges, weapons, rumours, threatened relatives, and the sudden disappearance of dependable public protection. Violence expanded through decisions, but those decisions were made inside a political world that had marked Tutsi as enemies and weakened the possibility that state power would restrain private aggression. Rwanda had built offices, identity cards, roads, and administrative hierarchies capable of limiting violence. In 1994, those capacities were redirected against the people they might have protected.

A comparison among Rwanda, the Cuban Missile Crisis, and the Maji Maji rebellion begins with a difficulty rather than a formula. Each case contains fear, authority, group identity, and the possibility that a local act will produce consequences beyond the actor’s immediate view. None presents the same kind of violence. Rwanda involved the organised persecution and mass killing of Tutsi and of Hutu who opposed or resisted the killers. The Cuban crisis brought the United States and the Soviet Union to the edge of confrontation involving nuclear weapons in October 1962. The Maji Maji rebellion opposed German colonial rule in what is now Tanzania from 1905 to 1907, and the German response included scorched-earth measures and the destruction of food supplies. Calling all three examples “aggression” is useful only if the word remains a starting point rather than a conclusion.

Rwanda shows how administrative identity can become a weapon when political leaders and local officials define a population as an internal enemy. The identity card, the roadblock, and the radio message belonged to different parts of one process: classification, controlled movement, and persuasion. The Cuban Missile Crisis presents a different danger. There, the destructive force of weapons helped produce caution at the highest level, even as secrecy, miscalculation, military pressure, and competing objectives made the situation perilous. President John F. Kennedy’s Executive Committee debated reconnaissance photographs, Soviet missiles in Cuba, naval quarantine, and air strikes. The possibility that events might move beyond presidential control remained present in the discussion. Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev faced pressures of his own, shaped by military and political considerations. Their restraint was a choice made under fear, not evidence that fear naturally produces peace.

The Maji Maji rebellion complicates any account that treats economic hardship as a direct cause of violence. German demands for labour, taxes, and agricultural production pressed deeply into rural life. Cotton cultivation tied local households to a colonial economy whose benefits and burdens were unequally distributed. Deprivation alone did not dictate insurrection. People joined through local political ties, religious authority, opposition to German officials, and the promise associated with maji medicine. The water believed by some followers to provide protection from German bullets gave resistance a shared language, but it did not make every community act alike. German reprisals burned crops and villages, transforming the consequences of rebellion and contributing to famine and mass death. These cases establish that fear has no single political result. In Kigali, it was organised against a designated population. In Washington and Moscow, it encouraged leaders to search for a way to withdraw without humiliation, though that search depended on communications, secrecy, military discipline, and cautious interpretation of an opponent’s actions. In German East Africa, fear and resentment fed resistance, while colonial officers answered a challenge to their rule by attacking the material basis of rebellion. Across the cases, fear became historically consequential through the people and offices that named its object, distributed warnings, and determined what conduct was permitted.

Technology altered each situation without supplying its motives. The nuclear missile did not create the purposes of the Cuban crisis; it changed the cost of a mistake and compressed the time available for decision. Radio in Rwanda helped spread messages and accusations, but radio alone did not define Tutsi as enemies, create roadblocks, or arm local participants. Maji Maji beliefs gave resistance a form that colonial officials could not easily control, but belief alone did not explain why some communities rebelled, why others hesitated, or why German reprisals became so destructive. A new device or system widens the reach of an existing choice only when institutions and political ideas give it direction.

Comparison also has to resist placing leaders at the centre of every explanation. Kennedy and Khrushchev mattered, as did the officials who carried their decisions into military systems. Rwanda’s interim government mattered, as did the local authorities and civilians through whom persecution became immediate. In Maji Maji country, religious figures and village leaders occupied different positions from cultivators, labourers, and colonial agents. A leader’s order may open a path, but it does not tell us who walks it, who blocks it, who profits, or who suffers. Large violence is assembled from encounters that are not interchangeable: the official reading an identity card, the soldier guarding an intersection, the cultivator deciding whether to join a rebellion, the commander interpreting a report.

A broad comparison can correct narrow explanations. If Rwanda is treated only as an eruption of ancient ethnic hatred, the work of identity documents, local administration, radio, militias, and political decisions disappears. If the Cuban crisis is treated only as a triumph of wise statesmanship, the danger created by secrecy, military plans, and nuclear deployment is softened. If Maji Maji is treated only as irrational religious rebellion, the material demands of German rule and the political meaning of colonial coercion vanish. Each reduction removes the conditions that gave the event its particular shape.

Historical evidence is strongest when a claim remains attached to a trace. A roadblock, a ministerial decision, a reconnaissance image, a broadcast, a tax demand, a burned field, or testimony from Kibuye can anchor an explanation. The anchor does not hold every conclusion. It holds a bounded one: this institution existed, this order was issued, this person or group encountered this danger, or this technology altered the range of possible action. Comparison can identify recurrent pressures from such particulars, but recurrence is not a law of human conduct.

The aftermath of Rwanda made the question of evidence unavoidable because survivors and the new government had to live among perpetrators, absentees, returning refugees, and graves. After the Rwandan Patriotic Front took control in July 1994, the country’s prisons filled with people accused of genocide crimes. Ordinary courts could not process the enormous number of cases, and the government turned towards gacaca, a revived and transformed form of community-based justice. Beginning in the early 2000s, gacaca courts brought cases into local communities, where judges and witnesses addressed killings, assaults, property destruction, and the concealment or removal of bodies.

A survivor might identify a person who had attacked a family member, describe the seizure of a house, or explain what happened at a church or on a road. A defendant might confess, deny, name others, or ask forgiveness. The proceedings could locate responsibility more precisely than a general account of collective guilt. They could also return stolen property or clarify the fate of people who had disappeared. Their public setting placed witnesses and accused persons in the same communities, sometimes where fear, dependence, or hostility had not ended.

Truth spoken in public did not automatically become reconciliation.

Gacaca carried several purposes at once: processing cases, establishing facts, punishing offenders, and making continued social life possible. Those purposes did not always fit together. A confession might be encouraged by the prospect of reduced punishment, while a survivor might regard the sentence as inadequate. Community participation widened the number of people able to speak, yet local pressure could shape what was said. The courts produced a vast record of accusation and testimony, but that record belongs to a process designed for justice after catastrophe, not to an untouched view of the catastrophe itself.

Refugee return brought another set of decisions. In 1994, large numbers of Hutu fled Rwanda, including civilians frightened by the advance of the Rwandan Patriotic Front and people connected to the defeated government, the army, or the forces that had carried out genocide. Many crossed into neighbouring states, where refugee camps became places of shelter, political organisation, disease, and armed activity. Some returned soon after the new government established control. Others remained for years. Some returned under pressure or after the camps were attacked and dismantled. “Return” described movement across a border; it did not describe one political experience.

Families coming back found houses occupied, damaged, or claimed by others. Survivors and returnees had to negotiate land, memory, suspicion, and the presence of people accused of participating in the genocide. A government that promised security also demanded loyalty and pursued those it considered responsible for crimes or renewed rebellion. The distinction between civilian and combatant could be difficult to maintain in camps where former soldiers and militia members operated among refugees. Borders therefore carried the violence outward, while the return of civilians brought its consequences back into Rwandan villages.

In eastern Zaire, later renamed the Democratic Republic of the Congo, camps near the Rwandan border became part of a wider armed struggle. In 1996, Rwandan and allied forces attacked the camps and supported an advance against Mobutu Sese Seko. The First Congo War ended with Mobutu’s overthrow in 1997 and Laurent-Désiré Kabila’s seizure of power. The war cannot be explained only as a continuation of Rwanda’s genocide. Congolese political conflicts, Mobutu’s weakened state, local disputes over land and citizenship, and the interests of neighbouring governments shaped it. Yet the refugee camps and the armed networks within and around them made the consequences of 1994 regional.

Violence travelled through people, weapons, administrative weakness, and political calculation. The Rwandan government sought to remove a security threat beyond its frontier. Congolese rebels sought to overthrow Mobutu. Neighbouring states pursued their own interests. Civilians in North and South Kivu bore the cost of campaigns that joined local grievances to regional power. The First Congo War did not close the history of 1994; it showed how an attempt to secure a state after mass violence could help generate war in another state.

A return from war to law is never a return to conditions before war. A gacaca hearing, a refugee convoy, and an army crossing into Zaire each addressed the past while producing new relations of power. Punishment could protect a community from impunity while deepening the authority of the government that decided who was dangerous. Border security could prevent armed attacks while exposing refugees and foreign civilians to military action. In the Cuban crisis, restraint prevented one catastrophe; in the Great War, a decision made through mobilisation schedules narrowed the time for restraint. After Rwanda, every choice remained entangled with choices elsewhere.

What can historical knowledge do when people are afraid? It can make certain warning signs easier to recognise: neighbours converted into categories, emergency language used to suspend ordinary protections, political identity armed, and refugees treated as evidence of collective guilt. It can show that roadblocks do not become lethal by accident, that camps may become military spaces without every refugee becoming a soldier, and that a weapon changes the consequences of a decision without supplying its purpose.

Officials cannot know exactly when a crisis will become mass violence. Evidence arrives unevenly, motives conflict, and actors conceal their intentions even from allies. The historian sees a sequence after it has acquired an ending; officials must decide while the sequence remains open. Comparing Rwanda, the Cuban Missile Crisis, and Maji Maji can discipline judgment by preserving differences and exposing false inevitabilities. It cannot turn uncertainty into foresight.

The unresolved question is whether that discipline can reach a person who must choose under fear: an official at a roadblock, a commander receiving a doubtful report, a village leader hearing that an army is approaching, or a president deciding whether to strike. If historical knowledge improves those choices, it will do so without predicting violence as weather. It will widen attention to the institutions and identities through which fear is made dangerous, and keep open the possibility that the decision has not yet been made.
